name: ragged tarp tent seen from above: a patched tarp thrown over a ridge pole on two upright poles, both sloped tarp planes visible from above, open front end showing a crate inside, guy ropes to stakes
label: wasteland_ruins/tent-tarp

surfaces.part: tarp roof, both sloped planes with ridge line

answer.evidence: The silhouette widens steadily from 3 px at row 0 to 30 px at row 12, which is a triangular tarp roof. Both sloped planes are visible, split by a light ridge line at x=16 (rows 3-15) with patches on each side. The tarp ends at an edge around rows 19-20, followed by 1-2 rows of dark eave shadow (x=23 rows 20-21 are darkest). Below that the open front shows a dark interior and a crate across rows 22-27, giving a front face of about 8 rows. Poles and stakes extend above and below the body (rows 0-3 and 28-31). The roof planes are the main top surface, so this reads as three-quarter view.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are close to the references: 13 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels. The outline is therefore a tinted dark teal/brown, not a sticker-style black line. But the whole piece uses only 20 distinct colours, against 66 and 185 in the references. The two tarp planes read as roughly 3-4 teal steps with a few patch marks, while the references carry about 5-6 steps per material. The tarp planes and the dark interior still contain small flat fills (10% near-flat coverage against 0% in both references). There is no per-tile highlighting or grain like the roof-tile scallops and stone shading in the references. Tile information density is therefore a little lower than the Beodeul standard, and when in doubt this fails.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small tent of about 2x2 tiles. Its outline is a dark teal that follows the tarp and a dark brown that follows the wood, so it does not read as a black sticker line. The measured near-neutral share of dark edge pixels is 0%, against 7-9% on the references. It has 13 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 on the references. Near-flat coverage is 10%, which is low and shows the tarp planes carry patches, seams and shading variation. Tarp shading is about 4 steps, a little under the references' 5-6, and the texture is patch and seam detail rather than the per-tile scallop grain of the roofs. The crate and ropes add small, separate details. Overall it sits at the reference's level of information density on the primary facts, with only mildly shallower ramps, so I pass it.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small teal tarp tent. On the measured facts it matches or beats both references: 13 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so its outline is a tinted dark teal/brown rather than a black sticker line. Near-flat coverage is 10% against 0% for the references. That is a small amount, likely a few tarp-plane patches, and it is not a large flat fill.
